title: ELAN — timing of anticoagulation after AF-associated stroke
question: How did earlier DOAC initiation compare with a later schedule?
population: 2,013 people with acute ischemic stroke and atrial fibrillation.
comparison: Earlier: within 48 hours for minor/moderate stroke or days 6–7 for major stroke. Later: days 3–4, 6–7 or 12–14, respectively.
result: The 30-day composite of recurrent ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, major extracranial bleeding, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage or vascular death was 2.9% versus 4.1% (risk difference −1.18 percentage points; 95% CI −2.84 to 0.47). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage was 0.2% in both groups.
limits: The confidence interval includes no difference. Trial severity categories and exclusions require review; this is not an automatic start-date rule.

sources.title: ELAN primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: OPTIMAS — early versus delayed DOAC initiation
question: Was initiation within four days noninferior to starting at 7–14 days?
population: 3,621 analyzed adults with AF-associated ischemic stroke at 100 UK hospitals; clinicians were uncertain about timing.
comparison: DOAC initiation within four days versus days 7–14.
result: At 90 days, recurrent ischemic stroke, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage, unclassifiable stroke or systemic embolism occurred in 3.3% of each group. Noninferiority met the two-percentage-point margin; superiority was not demonstrated. Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage was 0.6% versus 0.7%.
limits: Open-label treatment with masked adjudication. Apply the trial selection criteria; identical observed rates do not prove identical individual risk.

sources.title: OPTIMAS primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM. January 2025 publisher correction checked: wording and figure-at-risk count corrected; no endpoint change stated.

title: CATALYST — pooled randomized evidence on DOAC timing
question: What does pooled participant-level evidence show about earlier initiation?
population: 5,441 participants from TIMING, ELAN, OPTIMAS and START; median NIHSS 5. Primary outcome data were available for 5,429.
comparison: DOAC initiation within four days versus day five or later; individual participant data meta-analysis.
result: At 30 days, recurrent ischemic stroke, symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage or unclassified stroke occurred in 2.1% versus 3.0% (OR 0.70; 95% CI 0.50–0.98). Symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage was 0.4% in each group.
limits: This synthesis includes ELAN and OPTIMAS participants; it is not an independent additional randomized trial. Results retain the component trials’ selection limits.

sources.title: CATALYST primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: POINT — acute dual antiplatelet benefit and bleeding
question: What was the benefit–bleeding tradeoff of adding clopidogrel?
population: 4,881 patients with minor ischemic stroke or high-risk TIA at international sites.
comparison: Clopidogrel plus aspirin versus aspirin alone for the 90-day trial period.
result: Major ischemic events (ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction or ischemic vascular death) occurred in 5.0% versus 6.5% at 90 days (HR 0.75; 95% CI 0.59–0.95). Major hemorrhage occurred in 0.9% versus 0.4% (HR 2.32; 95% CI 1.10–4.87).
limits: Stopped early. Most ischemic events occurred in the first week; the 90-day design alone does not establish the optimal DAPT duration or eligibility for other stroke populations.

sources.title: POINT primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: SAMMPRIS — medical management versus intracranial stenting
question: Did adding Wingspan stenting improve outcomes in severe symptomatic intracranial stenosis?
population: 451 patients with recent TIA or stroke attributed to 70–99% stenosis of a major intracranial artery.
comparison: Aggressive medical management plus angioplasty/Wingspan stenting versus aggressive medical management alone.
result: Stroke or death by 30 days was 14.7% with stenting versus 5.8% with medical management. Estimated one-year primary-event rates were 20.0% versus 12.2%; that endpoint included early stroke/death and later qualifying-territory stroke.
limits: Enrollment stopped for safety concerns. This tested a specified stent strategy; it does not directly test balloon angioplasty alone or every later device and selection strategy.

sources.title: SAMMPRIS primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract and corrected NEJM report read; source updated July 2012. Protocol and supplements not reviewed.

title: CLOSE — PFO closure in selected cryptogenic stroke
question: Does PFO closure reduce recurrent stroke in patients with high-risk PFO features?
population: 663 patients aged 16–60 with recent stroke attributed to PFO and an atrial septal aneurysm or large shunt.
comparison: Closure plus antiplatelet therapy versus antiplatelets alone; the study also included a separate anticoagulation comparison.
result: Over mean follow-up of 5.3 years, stroke occurred in 0/238 closure patients versus 14/235 antiplatelet-only patients (HR 0.03; 95% CI 0–0.26). Procedural complications occurred in 5.9%; AF occurred in 4.6% versus 0.9%.
limits: Selected younger population with an attributed PFO mechanism. These findings do not make an incidental PFO an indication for closure or establish closure superiority to anticoagulation.

sources.title: CLOSE primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: TREAT-CAD — aspirin versus anticoagulation for dissection
question: Was aspirin noninferior to a vitamin K antagonist after cervical dissection?
population: 194 adults with symptomatic, MRI-confirmed cervical artery dissection within two weeks; 173 were analyzed per protocol.
comparison: Aspirin versus a vitamin K antagonist for 90 days.
result: The clinical/MRI composite occurred in 23% versus 15% (absolute difference 8 percentage points; 95% CI −4 to 21). Aspirin noninferiority was not established. Seven ischemic strokes occurred with aspirin and none with anticoagulation.
limits: Small open-label trial; the primary composite included MRI lesions at 14 days and clinical outcomes through 90 days. Failure of noninferiority does not establish universal anticoagulant superiority; DOACs were not tested.

sources.title: TREAT-CAD primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: SELECT2 — thrombectomy in selected large-core stroke
question: Does thrombectomy improve outcome in selected large-core anterior-circulation stroke?
population: 352 patients with ICA/M1 occlusion within 24 hours and ASPECTS 3–5 or imaging core ≥50 mL.
comparison: Thrombectomy plus medical care versus medical care alone.
result: The 90-day mRS distribution favored thrombectomy (generalized OR 1.51; 95% CI 1.20–1.89). Functional independence, a secondary outcome, was 20% versus 7%.
limits: Stopped early for efficacy; vascular complications occurred. Review complete selection criteria. The 2024 correction clarified core-volume measurement substitutions and stated that outcome direction and significance were unchanged.

sources.title: SELECT2 primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract and January 2024 publisher correction read; full trial report and supplements not reviewed.

title: BAOCHE — basilar thrombectomy at 6–24 hours
question: Does late-window basilar thrombectomy improve functional outcome?
population: 217 analyzed patients in China with basilar-artery stroke presenting 6–24 hours after symptom onset.
comparison: Thrombectomy plus medical treatment versus medical treatment alone.
result: At 90 days, mRS 0–3 occurred in 46% versus 24% (adjusted rate ratio 1.81; 95% CI 1.26–2.60). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage was 6% versus 1%; procedural complications occurred in 11% of thrombectomy recipients.
limits: Stopped at an interim analysis. The primary endpoint changed from mRS 0–4 to 0–3; the original endpoint did not show a conclusive difference. Review the trial’s full clinical/imaging selection rather than applying its time window alone.

sources.title: BAOCHE primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: DISTAL — medium and distal vessel thrombectomy
question: Does EVT improve disability after selected medium/distal vessel occlusion?
population: 543 participants within 24 hours; nondominant/codominant M2 or selected more distal MCA, ACA or PCA occlusions. Median NIHSS was 6.
comparison: EVT plus best medical treatment versus best medical treatment alone.
result: The 90-day mRS distribution did not improve significantly (common OR 0.90; 95% CI 0.67–1.22). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage was 5.9% versus 2.6%; mortality was 15.5% versus 14.0%.
limits: A neutral trial in its selected vessel/severity population; it does not establish equivalence or settle every medium-vessel treatment question. Dominant M2 was outside the stated M2 population.

sources.title: DISTAL primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: ESCAPE-MeVO — thrombectomy benefit and safety
question: Does EVT improve excellent functional outcome after medium-vessel occlusion?
population: 530 patients in five countries within 12 hours of last known well, with favorable baseline imaging; most occlusions were MCA branches.
comparison: EVT plus usual care versus usual care alone.
result: At 90 days, mRS 0–1 occurred in 41.6% versus 43.1% (adjusted rate ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.79–1.15). Mortality was 13.3% versus 8.4% (adjusted HR 1.82; 95% CI 1.06–3.12); symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage was 5.4% versus 2.2%.
limits: No primary-outcome benefit in this population. Vessel definition, imaging and time window matter; do not extrapolate large-vessel benefit automatically or infer a universal rule from one trial.

sources.title: ESCAPE-MeVO primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: ENRICH — early minimally invasive ICH evacuation
question: Does early minimally invasive evacuation improve recovery after selected ICH?
population: 300 patients with lobar or anterior basal ganglia ICH of 30–80 mL; treatment assignment within 24 hours.
comparison: Minimally invasive evacuation plus guideline-based medical management versus medical management alone.
result: Mean utility-weighted mRS (0–1; higher is better) at 180 days was 0.458 versus 0.374 (difference 0.084; 95% Bayesian credible interval 0.005–0.163). The benefit appeared attributable to lobar hemorrhage; 30-day mortality was 9.3% versus 18.0%.
limits: Adaptive enrollment later restricted inclusion to lobar ICH. Findings concern the tested technique, timing and selected population, not all ICH surgery. Postoperative rebleeding with deterioration occurred in 3.3%.

sources.title: ENRICH primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: ANNEXA-I — hemostatic efficacy and thrombotic harm
question: What were andexanet’s efficacy and safety tradeoffs in factor Xa inhibitor-associated ICH?
population: 530 patients with acute ICH after factor Xa inhibitor use within 15 hours; the interim efficacy analysis included 452.
comparison: Andexanet versus usual care; 85.5% of usual-care patients received PCC.
result: Composite hemostatic efficacy was 67.0% versus 53.1% (adjusted difference 13.4 percentage points; 95% CI 4.6–22.2). Thrombotic events occurred in 10.3% versus 5.6%, including ischemic stroke in 6.5% versus 1.5%. No appreciable difference in 30-day mRS or mortality was reported.
limits: Hemostatic efficacy is not functional benefit. This historical trial does not establish current drug availability or the preferred reversal pathway.

sources.title: ANNEXA-I primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: PRESTIGE-AF — anticoagulation after ICH with AF
question: How did DOACs change ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke risk after ICH?
population: 319 survivors of spontaneous ICH with AF, an anticoagulation indication and mRS ≤4; median follow-up 1.4 years.
comparison: A DOAC versus no anticoagulation.
result: First ischemic stroke favored DOACs (HR 0.05; 95% CI 0.01–0.36), while recurrent ICH noninferiority was not established (HR 10.89; 90% CI 1.95–60.72). All-event rates per 100 patient-years were 0.83 versus 8.60 for ischemic stroke and 5.00 versus 0.82 for ICH.
limits: The ischemic benefit and hemorrhagic harm require individualized assessment; this trial does not establish a universal restart date. Two indexed corrections could not be fully accessed.

sources.title: PRESTIGE-AF primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM. March and June 2025 corrections identified; publisher correction bodies inaccessible (403). No full corrected-report review.

title: MIND — minimally invasive evacuation at up to 72 hours
question: Did the Artemis evacuation strategy improve disability or survival?
population: 236 adults aged 18–80 with 20–80 mL supratentorial ICH, NIHSS ≥6 and GCS 5–15; 69.5% had primarily deep hemorrhage.
comparison: Minimally invasive surgery within 72 hours plus medical management versus medical management alone.
result: There was no demonstrated improvement in 180-day ordinal mRS (OR 1.03; 96% CI 0.62–1.72). Thirty-day mortality was 7.2% versus 9.8% (difference −2.5 percentage points; 95% CI −11.7 to 4.8).
limits: Enrollment stopped early after a feasibility analysis. Imprecision limits conclusions; do not treat the result as proof of equivalence or interchange its technique and timing with ENRICH.

sources.title: MIND primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: SWITCH — decompression for severe deep ICH
question: Does decompressive craniectomy improve outcome in severe deep ICH?
population: Adults aged 18–75 with severe basal ganglia or thalamic ICH; 197 randomized participants gave delayed consent.
comparison: Decompressive craniectomy plus best medical treatment versus best medical treatment alone.
result: At 180 days, mRS 5–6 occurred in 44% versus 58% (adjusted risk ratio 0.77; 95% CI 0.59–1.01; p=0.057). The report characterized the evidence as weak.
limits: Stopped early for funding; survival often involved severe disability. This is a decompression study in deep ICH, not evidence for every hemorrhage location or evacuation technique. Two indexed correction bodies were inaccessible.

sources.title: SWITCH primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM. June and July 2024 corrections identified; publisher correction bodies inaccessible (403). No full corrected-report review.

title: ORIENTAL-MeVO — thrombectomy in selected medium-vessel stroke
question: Did thrombectomy improve function in moderate-to-severe MeVO stroke?
population: 563 adults at 48 Chinese centers; eligible NIHSS ≥6 and presentation within 24 hours.
comparison: Thrombectomy plus medical management versus medical management.
result: At 90 days, mRS 0–2 occurred in 58.6% versus 46.6% (adjusted rate ratio 1.24; 95% CI 1.07–1.44). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage was 4.7% versus 2.2%; mortality 11.1% versus 10.2%.
limits: Open-label, single-country trial. The prespecified binary endpoint replaced ordinal mRS after its proportional-odds assumption failed. Interpret alongside neutral MeVO trials; selection differences do not establish a universal EVT rule.

sources.title: ORIENTAL-MeVO primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: SPARCL — atorvastatin after stroke or TIA
question: Did high-dose atorvastatin reduce recurrent stroke?
population: 4,731 patients with stroke/TIA 1–6 months earlier, LDL 100–190 mg/dL and no known coronary heart disease.
comparison: Atorvastatin 80 mg daily versus placebo.
result: Over median 4.9 years, fatal/nonfatal stroke occurred in 11.2% versus 13.1% (adjusted HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.71–0.99). Hemorrhagic strokes numbered 55 versus 33. Liver-enzyme elevations were more common with atorvastatin; overall mortality was similar.
limits: A selected secondary-prevention population. Net stroke benefit does not settle lipid treatment for every ICH survivor or establish a patient-specific hemorrhage risk.

sources.title: SPARCL primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM. Publisher 2018 correction checked: baseline Table 1 SE/SD labeling, with no outcome revision stated; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: Treat Stroke to Target — LDL goals after atherosclerotic stroke
question: Did a lower LDL target reduce major cardiovascular events?
population: 2,860 patients with recent ischemic stroke/TIA and cerebrovascular or coronary atherosclerosis in France and South Korea.
comparison: LDL target below 70 versus 90–110 mg/dL, using statin, ezetimibe or both.
result: Over median 3.5 years, ischemic stroke, MI, urgent coronary/carotid revascularization or cardiovascular death occurred in 8.5% versus 10.9% (adjusted HR 0.78; 95% CI 0.61–0.98). Intracranial hemorrhage and new diabetes did not differ significantly.
limits: Stopped administratively before the planned event count. This composite is broader than recurrent stroke; nonsignificant safety differences do not prove equivalence. The trial did not test a target below 55 mg/dL.

sources.title: Treat Stroke to Target primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; online publication 2019, print issue 2020. Full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: SPS3 — blood-pressure targets after lacunar stroke
question: Did a systolic target below 130 reduce recurrent stroke?
population: 3,020 patients with recent MRI-defined symptomatic lacunar infarction; mean follow-up 3.7 years.
comparison: Systolic BP below 130 versus 130–149 mmHg; achieved means at one year were 127 and 138 mmHg.
result: The primary all-stroke reduction was not statistically significant (HR 0.81; 95% CI 0.64–1.03). Intracerebral hemorrhage was reduced (HR 0.37; 95% CI 0.15–0.95). Treatment-related serious adverse events were infrequent.
limits: Open-label factorial trial. The ICH component does not convert the neutral primary endpoint into proven all-stroke benefit. This is the BP comparison, separate from the SPS3 antiplatelet comparison and from acute BP management.

sources.title: SPS3 blood-pressure comparison primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM. Indexed correction identifies addition of an author; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: PROGRESS — blood-pressure lowering after stroke or TIA
question: Did a perindopril-based regimen reduce recurrent stroke?
population: 6,105 people with previous stroke/TIA, including hypertensive and non-hypertensive participants.
comparison: Perindopril-based treatment, with indapamide at clinician discretion, versus matching placebo.
result: Over four years, fatal/nonfatal stroke occurred in 307/3,051 (10%) versus 420/3,054 (14%): relative risk reduction 28% (95% CI 17–38). Mean BP fell by 9/4 mmHg relative to placebo.
limits: A long-term regimen trial, not an acute BP target. Combination and single-drug strata were not a randomized comparison with each other. The abstract does not quantify detailed harms; indexed correction bodies were not fully accessible.

sources.title: PROGRESS primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM. Corrections indexed in Lancet 2001;358:1556 and 2002;359:2120 were not fully reviewed; detailed tolerability and correction effects remain unverified.

title: NAVIGATE ESUS — rivaroxaban versus aspirin
question: Did rivaroxaban prevent recurrent stroke in ESUS?
population: 7,213 patients with recent presumed embolic stroke without arterial stenosis, lacune or an identified cardioembolic source.
comparison: Rivaroxaban 15 mg daily versus aspirin 100 mg daily.
result: Over median 11 months, recurrent stroke/systemic embolism was 5.1% versus 4.8% per year (HR 1.07; 95% CI 0.87–1.33). Major bleeding was 1.8% versus 0.7% per year (HR 2.72; 95% CI 1.68–4.39).
limits: Stopped early for lack of efficacy and excess bleeding. This ESUS result does not address established AF or another definite anticoagulation indication.

sources.title: NAVIGATE ESUS primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: RE-SPECT ESUS — dabigatran versus aspirin
question: Did dabigatran reduce recurrent stroke after ESUS?
population: 5,390 patients with an embolic stroke of undetermined source; median follow-up 19 months.
comparison: Dabigatran 150 or 110 mg twice daily versus aspirin 100 mg daily.
result: Recurrent stroke was 4.1% versus 4.8% per year (HR 0.85; 95% CI 0.69–1.03); superiority was not demonstrated. Major bleeding was 1.7% versus 1.4% per year (HR 1.19; 95% CI 0.85–1.66); clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding was 1.6% versus 0.9% per year.
limits: Neutral superiority is not equivalence. The result does not establish benefit in retrospectively selected subgroups or apply to known AF.

sources.title: RE-SPECT ESUS primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: ARCADIA — atrial cardiopathy without AF
question: Did apixaban reduce recurrent stroke in atrial cardiopathy without AF?
population: 1,015 patients with cryptogenic stroke and atrial cardiopathy defined by ECG, NT-proBNP or indexed left-atrial diameter; no AF at randomization.
comparison: Apixaban, with dose reduction when indicated, versus aspirin 81 mg daily.
result: Recurrent stroke was 4.4% per year in both groups (HR 1.00; 95% CI 0.64–1.55). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 0 versus 7 patients; other major hemorrhage in 5 versus 5.
limits: Stopped for futility; mean follow-up 1.8 years. Small bleeding counts do not establish a safety advantage. Biomarker-defined atrial cardiopathy is distinct from documented AF.

sources.title: ARCADIA primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: CRYSTAL AF — prolonged monitoring after cryptogenic stroke
question: Did an insertable monitor increase AF detection?
population: 441 patients aged at least 40 with cryptogenic stroke, no AF on at least 24-hour ECG monitoring, randomized within 90 days.
comparison: Insertable cardiac monitor versus conventional follow-up.
result: The primary endpoint, detection of AF lasting over 30 seconds within six months, occurred in 8.9% versus 1.4% (HR 6.4; 95% CI 1.9–21.7). At 12 months, detection was 12.4% versus 2.0%.
limits: This was a detection trial, not proof of reduced recurrent stroke or a universal anticoagulation threshold for every device-detected episode. The abstract does not detail implantation harms.

sources.title: CRYSTAL AF primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: CREST-2 — revascularization for asymptomatic carotid stenosis
question: Did adding revascularization improve outcomes on intensive medical therapy?
population: Two parallel trials of asymptomatic stenosis ≥70%: 1,245 participants in the stenting trial and 1,240 in the endarterectomy trial.
comparison: Each procedure plus intensive medical management versus intensive medical management alone.
result: The four-year composite of stroke/death through day 44 or later ipsilateral ischemic stroke was 2.8% versus 6.0% with stenting (P=0.02), and 3.7% versus 5.3% with endarterectomy (P=0.24). Early events included seven strokes and one death with stenting versus none medically; nine versus three strokes in the endarterectomy trial.
limits: Separate trials did not compare stenting directly with endarterectomy. Results concern selected asymptomatic disease and include procedural harms; they do not establish a universal procedure choice.

sources.title: CREST-2 primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; online publication 2025, print issue 2026. Full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: ECST-2 — two-year interim carotid revascularization evidence
question: Did revascularization add benefit in lower-risk carotid stenosis?
population: 429 randomized patients with ≥50% asymptomatic or symptomatic stenosis and CAR-score predicted five-year ipsilateral stroke risk below 20%.
comparison: Optimized medical therapy alone versus medical therapy plus revascularization.
result: At two years, the hierarchical composite of periprocedural death/fatal stroke/fatal MI, nonfatal stroke, nonfatal MI and new silent infarction showed no difference (medical/procedure win ratio 1.01; 95% CI 0.60–1.70). One periprocedural death followed endarterectomy.
limits: Interim analysis with wide uncertainty, a selected risk population and an endpoint that includes silent infarction. It does not establish equivalence or negate benefit in higher-risk symptomatic disease.

sources.title: ECST-2 interim analysis primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM. January 2026 publisher correction checked: two appendix investigator names corrected; no outcome change stated. Full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: VNS-REHAB — paired stimulation for chronic arm weakness
question: Did paired vagus stimulation improve chronic upper-limb impairment?
population: 108 patients with moderate-to-severe arm weakness at least nine months after ischemic stroke.
comparison: Implanted active versus sham vagus stimulation paired with six weeks of rehabilitation; all participants received implants.
result: The primary Fugl-Meyer upper-extremity improvement immediately after therapy was 5.0 versus 2.4 points (difference 2.6; 95% CI 1.0–4.2). One serious surgery-related vocal-cord paresis occurred in the sham group.
limits: Small, selected chronic-stroke trial. The endpoint measures impairment, not independent living; both arms carried implantation risks. Trial efficacy does not establish individual candidacy, device availability or coverage.

sources.title: VNS-REHAB primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM; full report and supplements not reviewed.

title: AVERT — dose and timing of early mobilization
question: Did a higher-dose mobilization protocol within 24 hours improve recovery?
population: 2,104 adults with ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke meeting physiological criteria at 56 stroke units.
comparison: Frequent, higher-dose very early mobilization plus usual care versus usual stroke-unit care.
result: At three months, mRS 0–2 was less frequent with the intervention: 46% versus 50% (adjusted OR 0.73; 95% CI 0.59–0.90). Mortality was 8% versus 7% (OR 1.34; 95% CI 0.93–1.93). Nonfatal serious adverse events were 19% versus 20%.
limits: This tests a timing-and-dose package, not a mandate for bed rest or an isolated timing threshold. Most usual-care patients also mobilized within 24 hours. Detailed protocol and 2015 correction effects remain unverified.

sources.title: AVERT primary report
sources.access: Primary abstract read via PubMed/NLM. The 2017 correction changes licensing only; the 2015 correction body was inaccessible. Full protocol and supplements not reviewed.
